title: Weekend: Houthis hit Riyadh's Aramco Tower and target oil storage as Saudi supply risk grows
body: This is an escalation risk for crude rather than a confirmed supply loss: Saudi Arabia reports minor damage and intercepted missiles, and no outage has been reported. What matters is the direction. Aramco storage is now being targeted, and the Houthis have a declared maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, at a time when Hormuz flows are already disrupted and Saudi barrels routed via the Red Sea matter more for global supply. Coming on top of the suspected Iranian strike on Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and Rubio's warning that talks with Tehran are not productive, it strengthens the case for a firmer war-risk premium. Traders will be watching for any confirmed damage to Saudi output, storage or Red Sea loadings. --- A Houthi strike on Riyadh's financial district, with Aramco oil storage also in the crosshairs, shows the Iran war's reach now extends deep into the world's largest oil exporter, just as Saudi Red Sea exports matter most. Summary: Houthi forces struck the Aramco Tower in Riyadh's financial district on Saturday. The group said it also targeted Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities. Saudi Arabia said several missiles were intercepted and destroyed. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry reported minor damage and no casualties, though verified footage suggests heavier damage to at least one floor. The strike followed Houthi claims that a Saudi-led coalition air strike killed at least 33 people in Yemen.

title: RBA's Hunter warns AI could trigger sharp asset repricing as boom adds to inflation
body: Hunter's description of AI as a near-term inflationary force supports the RBA's tightening bias rather than pointing to relief. That underpins the Australian dollar on rate differentials and keeps the focus on the risk of further hikes. Her financial stability warning adds a central bank voice to growing market unease over AI valuations and funding, at a time when tech-linked assets are already under strain. Any further move toward repricing would favour defensive positioning in AI-exposed equities. It could also limit the Australian dollar's upside if global risk sentiment sours. --- Last week: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: RBA hikes to 18-year high --- The RBA sees AI as an inflation problem today and a potential financial stability problem tomorrow, with little sign yet of the productivity payoff that would justify the investment boom. Summary: RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said AI may be increasing risks to financial stability. Some asset prices could face sharp repricing, or disorderly adjustments, if returns on AI investment disappoint. There is limited evidence AI has materially lifted aggregate productivity or had large effects on employment in advanced economies. In the near term, AI-driven demand against constrained supply adds upward pressure on inflation. The long-run effect is likely broadly neutral. There are tentative signs of labour market adjustment in AI-exposed occupations, particularly for younger workers.

title: Rubio says Iran talks not productive as Tehran's demands are unacceptable
body: For oil, this is the more important signal of the weekend. Trump made avoiding renewed strikes conditional on progress in talks, and his Secretary of State now says there isn't any. That pushes escalation risk back toward the front of the market's mind and argues for a firmer war-risk premium in crude. Combined with the suspected Iranian strike on Iraq's Khor Mor gas field, the de-escalation story from Trump's CNN interview looks shakier. Traders are likely to be more cautious about selling crude on hopes of a deal. Any fresh threat to US forces or to Hormuz shipping would test Rubio's pledge to respond. Trump set progress in talks as the condition for holding off on new strikes, and his top diplomat is now saying that condition isn't being met, a shift that puts escalation risk firmly back in the frame. Summary: Rubio said negotiations with Iran are not productive because Tehran's demands are simply unacceptable. He said a diplomatic solution is sometimes not possible, though the US will keep exploring whether one exists. The US is taking defensive action and will respond if its forces in the region are threatened. Rubio stressed long-standing cross-party agreement that a nuclear-armed Iran would be completely unacceptable. The tone contrasts with Trump's weekend comments that renewed strikes were highly unlikely if talks progressed. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said negotiations with Iran are not productive because Tehran's demands are simply unacceptable.

body: The NZX 50 slipped 25 points, or 0.2%, to 13,974 in early Monday trading, extending the previous session's losses amid uncertainty over the general election outcome. The November 7 general election raised the prospect of a hung Parliament, though National appears best positioned to form a coalition with ACT and New Zealand First, while a narrow victory by the opposition bloc remains possible. Analysts noted that investors were also closely watching the US midterm election results, the evolving conflict in the Middle East, and their implications for oil prices. Traders were awaiting the latest Chinese consumer and producer price data, due later in the day. A positive session on Wall Street on Friday, driven by a rebound in technology stocks, helped limit the NZ market's decline. On the local bourse, healthcare and consumer staples names were the main drag on the index, while gains in financial and energy stocks helped cushion the fall. title: Qatar says US-Iran talks alive as Trump meets Qatari PM, oil swings on mixed signals
body: For crude, the Qatar meeting is the session's swing event. Signs of a credible path back to a ceasefire and nuclear talks would revive the selling seen at the open on Trump's CNN comments. If the gap over sanctions relief looks unbridgeable, as Rubio's comments suggest, escalation risk returns to the front. The weekend's strikes on Iraqi gas and Saudi infrastructure, continued disruption in Hormuz and Washington's tightening economic squeeze through Task Force Iron Gate all keep a floor under the war-risk premium. Until talks show concrete progress, headline-driven two-way swings look more likely than a sustained move in either direction. --- Oil spent the day caught between Trump's optimism and Rubio's pessimism, with Qatar now insisting a deal is still within reach and Trump's meeting with its prime minister the next test of whether diplomacy can outpace escalation. Summary: Qatar, mediating the talks, denied that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal, saying both sides are still working toward an agreement. Iran has reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington via Qatar, conditional on demands including sanctions relief. Trump meets the Qatari prime minister at 12:00 US Eastern, 17:00 GMT, to discuss a new ceasefire and resuming nuclear talks. Crude fell at the open on Trump's CNN comments, then recovered to around unchanged after Rubio's downbeat remarks.

title: WSJ: Japan spent a record $50 billion in one day to defend the yen, data confirms
body: The data confirms Tokyo will spend heavily, and alongside Washington, to defend the yen. That keeps intervention risk firmly in play as USD/JPY trades near 158, well within reach of this year's low near 164. It caps the upside for dollar-yen and makes long positions more two-way, including Morgan Stanley's carry-driven long USD/JPY call. Rate expectations remain the dominant driver, though: around 80% odds of a December Fed hike are keeping the gap wide, while a December BOJ move, supported by Ueda's upside-inflation comments, is the main path to narrowing it. Expect officials' rhetoric to sharpen if the pair approaches 160 again. --- Japan's record intervention numbers show how hard Tokyo, with Washington's help, fought the yen's slide, and how little lasting difference it made while the US-Japan rate gap stays wide. Summary: Japan spent a record $50 billion, almost 8 trillion yen, in a single day on July 30 to support the yen. Total intervention across July and August was around 15.4 trillion yen, roughly $97 billion, exceeding April and May. Finance Minister Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Bessent confirmed joint intervention in late July, the first since 1998. The yen had hit a four-decade low near 164 per dollar earlier this year and still trades around 158. Expectations of further Fed hikes are keeping the US-Japan rate gap wide. The BOJ raised rates to 1.25% in September and is expected to move again by year-end.

title: China extends suspension of 24% tariffs on US goods, keeps 10% levy ahead of APEC
body: This is a risk-positive development. Removing the chance of a tariff snapback gives some cushion to a market rattled by the AI sell-off and the weekend's Middle East escalation. It should support equities, the yuan and China-sensitive currencies such as the Australian dollar. It's continuity rather than fresh easing, though, so the upside is likely to be modest unless next week's APEC meeting delivers more. Agricultural markets, particularly soybeans, will look for signs that the truce extends to purchase commitments. --- Beijing has rolled over its tariff truce with Washington rather than let it lapse, removing a potential trade shock and setting a steadier tone for Trump and Xi's expected meeting at APEC next week. Summary: China's Ministry of Finance said it will continue suspending the 24% additional tariff on US goods. A 10% tariff on US goods will remain in place from November 10. The previous one-year suspension, agreed in November 2025, was due to expire this week. The move comes ahead of next week's APEC summit in China, where Trump expects to meet Xi. The decision maintains the status quo rather than marking further tariff relief. China will continue to suspend a 24% additional tariff on US goods while keeping a 10% levy in place from November 10, its Ministry of Finance said on Monday. The move extends a key element of the trade truce between Beijing and Washington just as the original arrangement was due to lapse.

title: Goldman's AI memory basket plunges 51% from peak, JPMorgan sees earnings buffer for now
body: The memory sell-off is the sharpest sign yet that investors are pricing a peak in the AI capex cycle before the earnings data confirms it. That keeps pressure on chip-heavy indexes such as the Kospi and on semiconductor names globally. JPMorgan's view that earnings are protected for six months gives value buyers a case for stepping in. Goldman's credit-spread warning, though, suggests the funding question could keep sentiment fragile, especially with tonight's Nvidia session adding to headline risk. Further widening in AI-linked credit spreads would be a signal that the equity downside isn't finished. --- Memory stocks have already halved from their peak on fears that the AI spending boom is cresting, yet JPMorgan says the earnings downturn the market is bracing for is still at least six months away. Summary: Goldman Sachs' AI memory stock basket has fallen 51% from its June peak, its deepest drawdown since ChatGPT launched. The basket had more than quadrupled in the year to that peak, driven by AI data centre demand and heavy positioning. Goldman had earlier warned that crowded positioning left memory stocks exposed to further liquidation. A Goldman strategist says AI cloud provider credit spreads are at their widest this year and that AI capex has likely peaked. JPMorgan says markets are pricing a memory downcycle as early as the first half of 2027. JPMorgan expects no earnings cuts over the next six months, citing long-term agreements and prepayments.

title: China October 2026 CPI +0.7% y/y (expected +0.8%, prior +0.9%)
body: A hot PPI and a soft CPI is a poor mix for China's growth outlook. It points to margin compression for manufacturers and weak domestic demand, which weighs on sentiment toward Chinese equities and keeps expectations of policy support alive. For the yuan, softer underlying inflation argues for easier policy at the margin, a mild negative. For the Australian dollar and commodity currencies, the read is mixed: firm producer prices reflect cost pressure rather than a demand-led recovery in China's appetite for raw materials. For oil, the PPI surge mainly shows the energy shock feeding through, not new demand strength. --- Earlier: China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities --- China's factories are facing their fastest price rises in years while consumer inflation slips further below 1%, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than any healthy reflation. Summary: China's October PPI rose 5.7% y/y, beating the 5.3% forecast and up from 5% in September. CPI rose 0.7% y/y, below the 0.8% expected and down from 0.9%. CPI was flat month-on-month, in line with forecasts, after a 0.2% rise in September. Core CPI eased to 0.8% from 1%, below the 0.9% forecast. The gap between producer and consumer inflation has widened to around five percentage points. Trade data is due Tuesday, with credit and money supply figures later in the week.

The bank's warning that higher oil prices could trigger systematic selling fits the way gold has traded through the Iran war: escalation lifts crude and yields, which weighs on bullion. Weekend strikes in Iraq and Saudi Arabia raise that risk this week. The heavy central bank bid underpins the longer-term case and is likely to cushion deeper dips. A shift toward Fed easing in late 2027 is the bank's main upside catalyst. --- Earlier: Gold ticks higher on softer oil, but Fed's 80% December hike odds cap gain --- Goldman has lowered its gold targets as Fed hikes erode hedging demand, but it is betting that relentless central bank buying will still carry bullion higher by the end of 2027. Summary: Goldman cut its end-2026 gold target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400. The bank cites a hawkish Fed, including an expected December hike, curbing demand for gold as a policy hedge. Central banks are expected to buy around 60 tonnes a month in 2026 and 2027. Current buying is estimated at around 85 tonnes. Central bank demand drives most of the roughly 15% upside Goldman forecasts by end-2027. A more hawkish Fed path could leave gold near $4,660 by end-2027, while fiscal worries could push it above the base case.

title: Gold ticks higher on softer oil, but Fed's 80% December hike odds cap gain
body: In this war, gold trades through the oil, inflation and rates channel rather than as a safe haven. That makes crude the key cross-asset signal: softer oil helps bullion, and renewed escalation hurts it. Weekend developments (Rubio's downbeat take on talks, the Khor Mor and Riyadh strikes, Hormuz disruptions) leave that support vulnerable if oil reprices higher. US CPI this week is the next test for December hike pricing, and therefore for gold's opportunity cost. Physical and official-sector buying should help limit dips, but they're unlikely to offset a further hawkish shift in rates on their own. Gold is being pulled between softer oil and bargain-hunting on one side and a hawkish Fed and global tightening on the other, with the Iran war acting through oil prices rather than as a safe-haven bid. Summary: Gold edged higher in Asia on Monday after a weekly gain of roughly 5%. Softer oil, after Trump played down new strikes on Iran, eased inflation concerns. Weekend escalation, including Rubio's comments and strikes in Iraq and Saudi Arabia, leaves oil, and therefore gold, exposed. Strong US payrolls and 4.1% unemployment lifted December Fed hike odds to around 80%, from about 70%. A former BOJ chief economist expects a December BOJ hike, adding to global tightening. Indian festival demand and central bank buying offer support, while a firm dollar remains a constraint.

title: Markets price three more BoE hikes, but analysts see a shallower path after move to 4%
body: The gap between futures pricing and analyst expectations is the key tension for UK assets. If the BoE delivers only one more hike, front-end gilt yields have room to fall and the curve could rally, which is why several analysts favour adding duration. For sterling, a shallower path than priced is a mild headwind on rate differentials. Analysts see little chance of the BoE out-tightening its peers, which limits the pound's upside. Oil is the swing factor: a sustained rise on Iran escalation, as this weekend's headlines threaten, would push the BoE back toward the market's hawkish pricing. --- investingLive European news wrap: BoE raises bank rate to 4.00% as expected --- The BoE has bought insurance against an energy-driven inflation spiral, but analysts broadly think markets are overpaying for further protection, with one more hike looking more likely than three. Summary: The BoE raised Bank Rate by 25bp to 4% in a unanimous vote, with inflation at 3.5% and rising. Markets price three more hikes by the end of next year, more than most economists expect. Many analysts see the move as a risk-management hike aimed at preventing second-round effects from the energy shock. One further hike, most likely in February, is the common base case, though some see the move as "one and done" if energy prices ease. Inflation is seen peaking at around 4.5% next summer, with the Iran war and oil prices the key risk.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6799 – Reuters estimate
body: Earlier: China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: Recap - BOJ's Ueda sees inflation near 2% but flags upside risks as energy costs bite
body: Ueda's acknowledgement of upside inflation risks, with energy costs set to push price growth higher into early next year, leans hawkish. It supports expectations that the BOJ will keep normalising policy, which is mildly supportive for the yen and keeps upward pressure on Japanese government bond yields. His comment that the BOJ watches other central banks closely, including their effect on exchange rates, keeps yen moves on the policy radar. Georgieva's warning on AI-related volatility adds to a theme already weighing on global tech this week. ---Ueda is comfortable that Japan has reached 2% underlying inflation, but with energy costs feeding through and upside risks building, the BOJ's job has shifted from getting there to holding the line. Summary: Ueda said the BOJ expects underlying inflation to stay around 2% but sees some upside risks. Energy-related price rises are feeding into consumer inflation, with price growth seen accelerating into early next year. Wages are growing at a pace consistent with 2% inflation, though the target has yet to become a social norm. The BOJ is watching other central banks closely, given their impact on exchange rates and interest rates. Unconventional tools could be used again if a severe shock hit, with care taken to limit side effects. IMF chief Georgieva said AI-related market volatility would complicate central banks' work. I was away from the desk on Friday, so I'm catching up on a few items worth revisiting.

title: China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities
body: The State Council's call reinforces the sense of a policy floor under Chinese equities. That should help cap downside volatility in mainland and Hong Kong shares, particularly at times of global risk aversion like the current AI-led wobble in tech.
